Leprosy

The ulcer trial found no additional healing, while one neuropathy trial cohort reported improvement in selected sensory and functional outcomes. Its later report comes from the same participants.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

The ulcer trial found no additional healing, while one neuropathy trial cohort reported improvement in selected sensory and functional outcomes. Its later report comes from the same participants.

Summary of the Evidence

Three publications address two distinct randomized cohorts. One 2010 trial studied chronic ulcers in people with leprosy sequelae. The other cohort enrolled 30 people for a physiotherapy comparison with or without PBM; its 2023 and 2025 articles share the same Brazilian trial-registration identifier and should be treated as two reports from one cohort, not as independent trials. No animal or separate in-vitro study of PBM for leprosy complications was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

In the 2010 ulcer trial, 25 of 51 assessed patients were randomized. The 97 ulcers had been present for a long time. After 12 weeks, ulcer area, depth, and PUSH healing scores did not differ significantly with laser compared with control, so this protocol did not add measurable healing benefit (Barreto and Salgado 2010).

The separate neuropathy trial compared physiotherapy alone with physiotherapy plus PBM in 30 participants over four weeks. Its 2023 report found better activity-limitation, pain, nerve-palpation, strength, and sensitivity measures in several domains for the combined group (Duarte et al. 2023). The 2025 report from the same registered cohort found fewer participants with severe activity limitation and improved median- and tibial-nerve functional measures in the PBM group. Pain scores improved in both groups without a between-group difference, and several quality-of-life domains improved in both groups (Bonazza et al. 2025). These findings are outcome-specific rather than evidence of a uniform effect across leprosy complications.

Animal evidence

No animal study directly examining PBM for leprosy-related neuropathy or ulcers was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No separate cell or tissue study directly testing these leprosy outcomes was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The ulcer trial used 660-nm red visible laser light at 2 J/cm² to the wound bed, three times weekly for 12 weeks. The neuropathy protocol used pulsed 904-nm near-infrared light at 70 mW, applied for nine seconds per point over 12 sessions in four weeks alongside physiotherapy. The local routes and treatment targets differ, and there was no dose-finding comparison.

Interpretation

The ulcer study found no additional healing with the tested red-light protocol. In the separate neuropathy cohort, selected activity, nerve, and functional measures improved, while pain improved in both groups without a between-group difference in the later report. Counting the two neuropathy articles as separate trials would exaggerate the amount of clinical evidence.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for selected nerve-function and activity outcomes with physiotherapy Very low for chronic ulcer healing
Publications and records3 publications from 2 randomized cohorts

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

One small ulcer trial found no added wound-healing benefit. A separate 30-person neuropathy trial reported improvements in several nerve and function measures with physiotherapy plus PBM; its 2023 and 2025 reports share the same registry and are not independent trials. A larger independently registered trial should confirm which outcomes improve and whether effects persist.
